Claude.notes: The Edison recorded-sound and Waymo Carcraft openings create the exact problem the three-families taxonomy answers — rare, rigorous narrative-concept pairing. Learners arrive at the distinction between synthetic, augmented, and mislabeled data themselves rather than being told. Lab executability depends on an operational chat backend, which is the module's only soft spot.
Claude.topIssue: Labs assume a working chat endpoint — no offline fallback or written worked example is offered if the assistant fails to load.

Gemini.notes: Definitions of synthetic vs augmented vs mislabeled data are clean and defensible. However, the HUGS (Human Gaussian Splatting) paper surfaced in later modules is commonly attributed to academic labs rather than Apple as a primary author, and the "tails disappear" result is attributed to Toronto/Cambridge here while other modules credit Edinburgh/Oxford — the Shumailov et al. affiliation should be unified across the course.
Gemini.topIssue: The 2024 "tails disappear" research is attributed to "Toronto and Cambridge," but the canonical model-collapse paper is Shumailov et al. from Oxford/Edinburgh — the attribution needs to match across modules.

Perplexity.notes: The lead examples — Waymo Carcraft 2020 stats, Phi-1 (2023), Alpaca (2023), early 2024 Llama 3 synthetic data — were current when authored but are now two to three years old. The conceptual frame holds up, but the "Scale and Prevalence in 2024" section reads as a dated snapshot rather than a current picture of where synthetic data sits in late-2026 frontier training.
Perplexity.topIssue: The "Scale and Prevalence in 2024" section stops at Llama 3 / Phi-3 and needs a 2025–2026 refresh covering post-o1 reasoning distillation and agentic training data pipelines.

modules.module: M2: Why Real Data Is Running Out

Claude.notes: The Epoch AI token-exhaustion paper, the NYT v. OpenAI lawsuit, and Chinchilla each anchor one of the four scarcity mechanisms the lesson lays out — story and concept are structurally coupled. The three-tier model of human text (web / books / expert) earns its place because the narrative has established the stakes.
Claude.topIssue: The four scarcity types (rarity, ethical/legal, annotation, distribution) from M1 are revisited but could be cross-referenced more explicitly so learners see the carry-over.

Gemini.notes: Technical claims are tight: Epoch AI's 2024 exhaustion paper is real and well-cited, Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al. 2022) is described accurately, and the Books3 removal timeline matches public record. The characterisation of "fair use remains unresolved" is still legally accurate as a doctrine statement.
Gemini.topIssue: The 250+ trillion raw token figure for Common Crawl is plausible but should name the specific snapshot/year and the pre-filter vs. post-filter delta to avoid being read as a single durable number.

Perplexity.notes: Material is unusually current relative to the rest of the course: EU AI Act (2024), NYT lawsuit, Books3 removal, and the Epoch AI timeline all remain the frame people reference in late 2026. The ongoing status of the NYT case and later copyright rulings should be referenced so learners don't treat the December 2023 complaint as the end of the story.
Perplexity.topIssue: The NYT v. OpenAI lesson frames the case as newly filed; by late 2026 it has progressed through discovery and summary judgment and should be presented as an evolving legal narrative, not a snapshot.

modules.module: M3: How Models Generate Training Data

Claude.notes: Each generation method — instruction pipelines, Constitutional AI, process reward models, debate — is introduced through a specific documented result (Alpaca, CAI, Let's Verify Step by Step). Learners can trace how the concept answers the problem opened in the scene. Density is slightly concept-heavy but defensible at this level.
Claude.topIssue: The transition from instruction pipelines (L1) to CAI (L2) is abrupt — a brief bridge paragraph showing why instruction tuning plateaued would strengthen the story arc.

Gemini.notes: The Alpaca 52,000 pairs / ~$500 and the Lightman et al. 2023 78%-vs-72% MATH figures match published numbers. ROUGE-L and Self-Instruct are defined precisely. This is the strongest module in the course on definitional precision.
Gemini.topIssue: The claim "Alpaca matched GPT-3 on many benchmarks" is slightly generous — the original Alpaca report compared qualitative judgments on a small eval, not benchmark parity; the phrasing should be tightened.

Perplexity.notes: The CAI, PRM, and Alpaca references are foundational and still cited in late-2026 practice, so the content is durable. What is missing is a current anchor: there is no mention of post-o1 process-reward-style training, Deliberative Alignment, or the 2025 wave of long-context synthetic reasoning datasets that would situate learners in today's pipelines.
Perplexity.topIssue: No post-2023 reference for how process reward models are actually used in production reasoning stacks today — the lesson stops at the original 2023 paper.

modules.module: M4: Quality Control for Synthetic Data

Claude.notes: The model-collapse opening sets up exactly the problem that filtering, diversity measurement, and human-in-the-loop lessons address. "Hallucination laundering" and "Oracle verification" are coined crisply and stay useful across the rest of the course. The lab prompts (diagnose Pipeline A with 90% recycled outputs) genuinely require the module's frameworks to answer.
Claude.topIssue: The four lessons (failure modes → filtering → diversity → human-in-the-loop) are strong individually but would benefit from a closing synthesis that ranks the four defenses by cost and effectiveness.

Gemini.notes: The Shumailov model-collapse paper is attributed to "Rice University and the University of Toronto" here but to Edinburgh/Oxford in modules 7 and 8 — one of these attributions is wrong, and the Nature 2024 version is the Oxford/Edinburgh group. The Llama 3 filtering description is plausible but not independently verifiable at the level of precision suggested.
Gemini.topIssue: Shumailov et al. institutional attribution conflicts with later modules; this inconsistency on a central citation needs to be resolved to the Oxford/Edinburgh group.

Perplexity.notes: The filtering and diversity frameworks remain current — MinHash LSH, Vendi Score, and quality classifiers are still the stack labs use. The Llama 3 example anchors the lesson in April 2024; a Llama 4 / Gemini 2.5 / Claude 4 update on how filtering has scaled would modernize this.
Perplexity.topIssue: Filtering stack is anchored on Llama 3 (April 2024) with no mention of how 2025–2026 frontier labs have evolved classifier-based quality control at scale.

Claude.notes: The SL-CAI / RLAIF phase split, the critique-revise loop, and the Claude 1 → Claude 3 trajectory are presented with first-person precision you rarely see in a generalist curriculum. Over-refusal is honestly named as a failure mode, not glossed. The Model Spec is placed correctly as the public descendant of the constitution.
Claude.topIssue: There is some overlap with M3 L2's CAI material — M5 L1 would read better if it explicitly acknowledged the handoff and promised the deeper treatment that follows.

Gemini.notes: CAI mechanics (SL-CAI supervised phase then RLAIF phase) are correctly separated, and the "16 principles" / Model Spec May 2024 references match the public record. The red-teaming → critique → revise → SFT pipeline is described with no technical errors I can flag.
Gemini.topIssue: The sycophancy limitation of self-critique is mentioned briefly in M7 but should also be surfaced here, where the critique-revise loop is first laid out in detail.

Perplexity.notes: The scaling arc stops at Claude 3 (March 2024) and the Model Spec (May 2024). In late 2026 there have been further model generations and extensive public commentary on how the constitution has evolved; the lesson reads as a frozen snapshot of the 2022–2024 arc.
Perplexity.topIssue: The Claude 1 → Claude 3 trajectory ends at March 2024 and does not extend to the current state of Anthropic's alignment stack, which a learner reading this in 2026 will notice immediately.

Claude.notes: The arc from Hinton's 2015 soft-targets framing, through DistilBERT (2019), to DeepSeek-R1 distillation (2025) is a satisfying three-beat story about the same underlying idea maturing. The distinction between response-based, feature-based, and sequence-level distillation is drawn clearly and the lab prompt uses it well.
Claude.topIssue: The Alpaca training cost is reported here as approximately $600, while M1/M2 report ~$500 — one of these needs to be corrected and standardised across the course.

Gemini.notes: The DistilBERT numbers — 40% fewer parameters, 97% of GLUE, 60% faster — match the published 2019 paper. The DeepSeek-R1 January 2025 release and the R1-Distill-Qwen-7B matching o1-mini on math are also accurate. The Alpaca cost discrepancy with earlier modules is the one factual rough edge.
Gemini.topIssue: Alpaca cost cited as ~$600 contradicts M1/M2's ~$500 — the actual published number was around $500 for the data-generation API spend; the figure needs to be made consistent.

Perplexity.notes: This is the most current-feeling module in the course — the DeepSeek-R1 January 2025 anchor puts learners inside the reasoning-distillation era rather than the 2022–2023 one. Speculative decoding and rejection-sampling distillation are correctly framed as live production techniques.
Perplexity.topIssue: DeepSeek-R1 is cited but there is no mention of how the distillation landscape evolved through 2025–2026 as other labs released reasoning models and open distilled variants.

Claude.notes: The grounded-loop vs closed-loop distinction is the module's best idea and does real work across the rest of the course — it gives learners a lens to classify any recursive-training claim they encounter. AlphaCode and AlphaGo Zero are well chosen as contrasting anchors. The CAI material in L3 is largely a reprise of M5's and should be trimmed or re-angled toward the recursive-improvement question specifically.
Claude.topIssue: L3 on CAI largely repeats M5's material rather than extending it to the recursive-improvement frame introduced in L1.

Gemini.notes: Shumailov's affiliation is finally rendered as Edinburgh here and Oxford in M8 — closer to the public attribution, though not fully consistent. AlphaCode (Feb 2022) and AlphaGo Zero (2017) framings are accurate, and "capacity ceiling" is a reasonable summary of the self-referential-training literature.
Gemini.topIssue: The Shumailov et al. paper is anchored to Nature 2024 here but to "Shumailov et al. (2023)" in other modules — the course should use one canonical form (the 2023 preprint vs the Nature 2024 version) consistently.

Perplexity.notes: Self-Rewarding LMs and SPIN get name-dropped in the lab but never in the lesson body, which is the one place where the module actually touches 2024-and-later recursive-improvement research. The CAI reprise in L3 costs the module pacing relative to M5.
Perplexity.topIssue: SPIN and Self-Rewarding Language Models appear only in a lab prompt; they should be introduced in the lesson text so learners encounter the 2024 state of RSI in the primary content, not an afterthought.

modules.module: M8: Where Synthetic Data Is Going

Claude.notes: As a capstone, the module threads scaling laws, process supervision, and agentic/tool-use training into a coherent "synthetic data as the alignment stack" argument. The Orca-13B framing lands the stake for domain-specialised distillation. Content overlap with M5 and M7 on CAI is the biggest flow issue.
Claude.topIssue: L2 (CAI + PRMs at scale) repeats material already covered in M3 and M5; this capstone module would benefit from leaning into agentic training and scaling frontier questions instead.

Gemini.notes: Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al., 2022), Kaplan et al. 2020 scaling laws, Shumailov et al. Oxford 2023, Lightman et al. 2023 for PRMs, and Microsoft Research Orca 2 (2023) are all accurately cited. Orca's "matched GPT-4 on several benchmarks" is broadly defensible but worth a precision note.
Gemini.topIssue: The claim that Orca (13B) "matched GPT-4 on several benchmarks" overstates the original paper's finding — Orca matched GPT-3.5/ChatGPT and approached GPT-4 on a subset; the phrasing should be tightened.

Perplexity.notes: A "Where It's Going" module should be the most forward-looking in the course, but it anchors on 2022–2023 citations (Kaplan 2020, Chinchilla 2022, Orca 2 2023, Lightman 2023). The agentic-AI framing in L3 is the right direction but reads as an opening, not a current snapshot; a learner reading this in late 2026 will not get a clear picture of today's research frontier.
Perplexity.topIssue: The capstone's "frontier" references stop in 2023, so the module does not actually describe where synthetic data is going now — it describes where it was going from a 2024 vantage point.
